title: 第四章 理论上的人民主权
originalTitle: 4 The Sovereignty of the People in Theory

zh: 本章将论证：人民——罗马人的 δῆμος、古老的
——在拜占庭拥有主权。这并非如许多罗马与拜占庭研究者所认为的那样只是一种好古的虚构，而是一个意识形态与历史事实：人民自己理解它，几乎所有皇帝也接受它，至少那些想保住皇位者如此。正如近来有人就古老共和国本身所写的那样，人民主权的证据“确实存在，但需要我们主动从史料中发掘并解释这些证据，既记得权势之人，也记得罗马人民”。
是时候给拜占庭共和国重新注入一些血液了，而且不只是隐喻意义上的血。这一努力将兑现第1章的承诺：提供一个自下而上的拜占庭政体模型，以制衡目前占主导的自上而下模型。本章通过考察若干关键事件，梳理出共和国各要素行为方式的更广泛意涵——即它们对政治行动视为理所当然的前提——以及这些行动在史料中如何被表述。
en: This chapter will argue that the people, the δῆμος of the Romans, the old

were sovereign in Byzantium. This was not a mere antiquarian fiction, as many scholars of Rome and Byzantium have thought, but an ideological and historical fact understood by the people themselves and accepted by almost all emperors, at least those who wanted to keep their throne. As has recently been written about the old Republic itself, the evidence for popular sovereignty “does exist, but it has to be rescued and interpreted with a conscious effort to remember not just the great and powerful but the Roman People too.”

It is time to put some blood back into the Byzantine republic, and not just the metaphorical kind. This effort will make good on the promise of Chapter 1 to provide a bottom-up model of the Byzantine polity that will act as a counterweight to the top-down one that currently prevails. Examining some key events, this chapter will tease out broader implications for how the various elements of the republic behaved—that is, what they took for granted regarding the political action—and how that action was represented in our sources.

zh: 本章介于迄今较理论性的讨论与随后较历史性的各章之间。它旨在提供一个主权模型，既契合拜占庭历史的事实，也契合我们的文本描述权力转移（尤其是暴力转移）的方式。暴力转移更能表明共和国的哪一个要素拥有在意识形态上无可争议的权利去决定应由谁来正当地行使权力。这些时刻通常也是法律运作被暂停的时刻，而且不只是涉及皇帝人身的法律（包括效忠誓言的效力与对其权威的合法服从）。它们是见证法律秩序崩溃的普遍“例外状态”。该秩序可能周期性瓦解，但人民决定谁有资格重建它的更根本权利却不会瓦解。这种紧急状态与皇帝权威自身在法律之外行动时所代表的那种状态恰成两极。拜占庭的政治史就在两者之间摆动。
en: This chapter transitions between the more theoretical discussion so far and the more historical chapters to follow. It aims to provide a model of sovereignty that fits the facts of Byzantine history as well as the way in which our texts describe transfers of power, especially violent ones. Violent transitions better indicate which element of the republic had the ideologically uncontested right to reassign the legitimate exercise of power. These were also moments when the operation of the law was usually suspended, and not only of the law relating to the person of the emperor (including the validity of oaths of allegiance and lawful deference to his authority). They were general “states of exception” that witnessed the breakdown of the legal order. That order may have periodically crumbled, but not so the more fundamental right of the people to determine who was entitled to reconstitute it. This state of emergency was the polar opposite to that represented by imperial authority itself when it acted outside the law. The political history of Byzantium oscillated between the two.

zh: 米海尔五世的兴起与覆灭
en: The Rise and Fall of Michael V

zh: 在提出共和主权模型之前，我先考察一段短暂统治的终结，它戏剧性地印证了上述论点。许多学者把这一事件视为反常、且意义仅限于其自身时代，但我认为它揭示了始终存在于拜占庭政治领域中的张力与前提，即便只是处于潜伏状态。第5章将聚焦人民主权在拜占庭的历史表现，并表明它们事实上是一种长期行为模式的一部分——事实上正是拜占庭政治的母体。
en: Before presenting a model for republican sovereignty, I will examine the end of a brief reign that dramatically illustrates the points made above. Many scholars present this event as aberrant and limited in significance to its own time, but I believe that it reveals tensions and assumptions that were always present in the Byzantine political sphere, even if only in a latent state. Chapter 5, which will focus on the historical manifestations of popular sovereignty in Byzantium, will show that they were in fact part of a longstanding pattern of behavior, the very matrix, in fact, of Byzantine politics.

zh: 我的出发点是1042年皇帝米海尔五世（Michael V）的倒台。

这一事件众所周知，其对君士坦丁堡权力平衡的惊人意涵亦然，但它通常被视为11世纪中期政治所特有，并被与所谓“城市阶级的兴起”相联系。而这种兴起又通常依据这一事件来界定，使论证陷入循环。拜占庭历史上其他人民（有时还有元老院）在帝国政治中扮演突出角色的时期，尤其是7、8世纪，也被研究那些时期的学者视为非典型。它们被纳入各自语境的叙述，却未被整合进对拜占庭政治领域的一般叙述。其效果（即便非其意图）是把民众行动边缘化为特例。一整系列类似事件由此被搁置、被边缘化。
事实上，无论11世纪君士坦丁堡在社会与经济层面发生着什么，1042年事件的

母体并不反常。该事件与同类其他事件的唯一区别在于：它被三位同时代人（或年代相去不远的作者）以戏剧性的细节叙述出来——普塞洛斯（Psellos）、阿塔莱亚特斯（Attaleiates）与斯基利齐斯（Skylitzes）。我本也可以用532年几乎推翻查士丁尼的尼卡暴动来达到同一目的，因为它揭示了关于谁有权做什么的相同底层前提——若非其结局的话：查士丁尼是唯一以如此规模对本国人民使用暴力者，这助成了他作为暴君的名声。在梳理米海尔五世生平与短暂统治中的事件时，我将突出那些在拜占庭大部分历史中可见运作的规范。它们与第3章所考察的484年维里娜（Verina）致安条克人民信背后的规范高度吻合。
en: My launching-point will be the fall of the emperor Michael V in 1042.

This event is well known, as are its alarming implications for the balance of power in Constantinople, but it is usually treated as distinctive to the politics of the mid-eleventh century and associated with an alleged “rise of the urban classes.” This rise is usually defined on the basis of this event, making the argument circular. Other periods of Byzantine history when the people (and sometimes the senate) took a prominent role in imperial politics, especially the seventh and eighth centuries, are also treated as atypical by scholars who focus on those periods. They are included in accounts of their individual contexts but not integrated into general accounts of the Byzantine political sphere. The effect, if not the intention, is to marginalize popular actions as idiosyncratic. A whole series of similar events are thereby bracketed off and marginalized.
In fact, whatever may have been happening both socially and economically in eleventh-century Constantinople, the

matrix of the events of 1042 was not atypical. The event in question differed from others in its class only in that it was narrated in dramatic detail by three contemporaries (or close enough): Psellos, Attaleiates, and Skylitzes. I could have used for this purpose the Nika riots that almost toppled Justinian in 532, as they reveal the same underlying assumptions about who had the right to do what, were it not for its outcome: Justinian was unique in using violence against his people on such a scale, which contributed to his reputation as a tyrant. As we move through the events in the life and brief reign of Michael V, I will highlight the norms that we can see operating throughout most of Byzantine history. They corresponded closely to the norms behind Verina’s letter to the people of Antioch in 484, examined in Chapter 3.

zh: 米海尔五世在两个王朝利益的交汇点上台。他是前任皇帝米海尔四世（Michael IV，帕夫拉戈尼亚人，1034–1041年在位）的侄子；而米海尔四世又是通过与佐伊（Zoe）——绵延多代的马其顿王朝的女继承人——结婚而登上皇位的。在其叔米海尔四世（作为皇帝颇受好评）去世前，未来的米海尔五世已被擢升至次于皇帝的
（凯撒）头衔，并被佐伊正式收为养子。这两次身份变动都发生在布拉赫奈（Blachernai）教堂的一次公开（δημοτελῆς）仪式上，所有职官亦出席。我们的史料普塞洛斯说，他受到全体在场者的欢呼，且还有与设立
相关的进一步仪式，但他未透露细节，因为读者对此早已熟知。
米海尔四世死后，佐伊发现自己独自掌握
。斯基利齐斯记载，她意识到自己无力承担治理
的重任，三天后决定擢升米海尔——他在公共事务
上精力充沛。
普塞洛斯补充说，这使因未来而悬心的都城安定下来。我们再次注意到：皇帝职分被视为公共行政的最高形式，其潜在担任者仅依此标准被评估。
以惯常的游行、加冕“以及随之而来的一切其余环节”被擢升至
之阶。普塞洛斯再次未透露细节——其中必定包括人民的欢呼。
关于迄今的叙述应注意两点：其一，佐伊的选择表面上主要依公共利益治理能力的标准；其二，我们被告知都城正在注视，显然对宫廷政治感兴趣。
en: Michael V came to power at the nexus of two dynastic interests. He was the nephew of the previous emperor, Michael IV the Paphlagonian (1034–1041), who had, in turn, been elevated to the throne by marriage to Zoe, heiress of the long-lived Macedonian dynasty. Before the death of his uncle Michael IV, who was well regarded as an emperor, the future Michael V had been elevated to the subordinate imperial rank of

and formally adopted by Zoe as her son. Both changes in his status occurred at a public (δημοτελῆς) ceremony at the Blachernai church that was attended by all office-holders as well. Our source, Psellos, states that he was acclaimed by all in attendance and that further ceremonies took place relating to the creation of a
but he does not divulge details, as they would have been well known to his readers.
When Michael IV died, Zoe found herself in sole possession of the
Skylitzes records that she realized that she was not up to the task of governing the
and, after three days, decided to elevate Michael, who was energetic when it came to public affairs

This, Psellos adds, calmed the City down, which was in suspense about the future. We note again that the imperial office was regarded as the highest form of public administration and its potential holder is evaluated by that criterion alone. The
was raised to the rank of
with the usual procession, coronation, “and all the rest that follows.” Psellos again does not divulge the details, which certainly included acclamation by the people.

We should note two things about the narrative so far: first, Zoe’s choice was ostensibly guided primarily by the criterion of competence in the administration of the public interests, and, second, we are told that the City was watching, obviously interested in the politics of the palace.

zh: 米海尔五世宣誓尊崇佐伊并尊重她的皇帝特权。作为奥古斯塔（Augusta），她被视为皇位继承人（两位米海尔都是通过她登上皇位的），“而且她普遍受欢迎，身为女性……她还以慷慨的馈赠赢得了所有人的心”。
米海尔五世在这宣誓一事上或许没有多少选择：正如我们将看到的，对公众舆论的感知几乎对皇帝行动施加了压倒性压力。我们很快就会看到民众的拥戴是多么重要的政治资本、公众舆论对保住皇位是何等关键的因素。新皇帝自己也着手培育舆论，赢得都城人民——“不仅是精英，还有平民与工匠”——授予他们“自由”。
他们对他如此拥戴，以致他开始以为可以废黜佐伊。据斯基利齐斯，米海尔“先试探市民，看他们对他持何种看法”。复活节后的星期日，他“试图在游行中探明公众舆论如何”。
庆典极为盛大，于是当夜他把佐伊流放至一座岛上并给她剃度。普塞洛斯说，米海尔告知元老院她阴谋反对他，然后“试图说服聚集的民众”。发现自己的话被支持者回声般附和，他“解散了那次集会”。
但不久之后“整个都城——我确实指所有人，不分性别、财产与年龄……都奋起而动，开始以小群行动，变得骚动不安”。他们开始发声反对他；公众舆论转恶。到第二天，显然这是一场要废黜他的民众运动。
en: Michael V swore oaths to honor Zoe and respect her imperial privileges. As an Augusta, she was regarded as the heir to the throne (it was through her that both Michaels had come to it), “and she was universally popular, being a woman... and she had also won over everyone’s heart through her generous gifts.”

Michael V may not have had much choice in the matter of this oath: as we will see, perceptions of public opinion exerted almost overwhelming pressure on imperial action. We will presently see what an asset it was to be popular and how critical a factor public opinion was for holding the throne. The new emperor began to cultivate public opinion himself, winning over the people of the City, “not only the elite but the commoners and the craftsmen too,” granting them “freedoms.”

They became so devoted to him that he began to think that he could oust Zoe. According to Skylitzes, Michael “tested the citizens first, to see what opinion they had of him.” On the Sunday after Easter “he attempted to ascertain what public opinion was” during the procession.

The festivities were splendid, so that night he exiled Zoe to an island and had her tonsured. Psellos says that Michael informed the senate that she had plotted against him and then “attempted to persuade the demotic crowd.” Finding that his words were being echoed back to him by his supporters, he “dissolved that assembly.”

But shortly thereafter “the entire City, and I do mean everyone regardless of sex, fortune, and age... roused itself and began to move in small groups, becoming tumultuous.” They began to speak against him; public opinion turned foul. By the second day, it was clear that this was a popular movement to depose him.

zh: 相比之下，阿塔莱亚特斯与斯基利齐斯记载米海尔派一名传令官到君士坦丁广场向人民宣读一份解释其行动的文件；斯基利齐斯把此事置于任何不满之前，而阿塔莱亚特斯更可信地置于不满之中，作为挽回舆论的尝试。无论哪种，群众都不接受，投掷石块并暴动。他们开始喊反对他的口号，“全体人民异口同声”高呼集结口号“挖出他的骨头”——这长期以来就是废黜皇帝的信号。
另一信号是呼喊“不配（ἀνάξιος）”，即不配皇位。
我们还会听到更多这个词。米海尔所剩选项无几。他召回佐伊，让她在紧邻皇宫的赛马场向民众露面。
但这使他们更加愤怒。他们迫使牧首站到自己一边，又把佐伊的妹妹塞奥多拉（Theodora）从修道院拉出来加入他们的事业，尽管她并不情愿。人民此时已接管整个都城，围攻皇宫并破门而入，米海尔逃往斯图迪奥（Stoudios）修道院，在那里依两姐妹之命被刺瞎。皇权通过民众行动恢复于两姐妹之手。
en: Attaleiates and Skylitzes, by contrast, have Michael send a herald to the forum of Constantine to read a document out to the people explaining his action; Skylitzes places this before any discontent, but Attaleiates, more plausibly, in the midst of it, as an attempt to win back public opinion. Either way, the crowd would have none of it, threw stones, and rioted. They began to chant slogans against him and “the entire people with one voice” shouted the rallying cry “Dig up his bones,” which had long been a signal for deposing an emperor.
This was signaled also by the chant “Unworthy (ἀνάξιος),” that is, of the throne.
We will hear more of this term. Michael had few options left. He recalled Zoe and presented her to the people in the hippodrome, next to the palace.

But this made them all the more angry. They forced the patriarch to side with them, and then pulled Zoe’s sister Theodora out of her convent to join their cause, though she was unwilling. The people had by now taken over the entire City, besieging the palace and breaking in, so Michael fled to the monastery of Stoudios, where by order of the two sisters he was blinded. Imperial power was restored through popular action to the two sisters.

zh: 我们的史料一致认为这是一场真正的民众起义，都城所有阶级都参与，甚至包括妇女。它并非由任何特定之人策划——两姐妹只是被卷入其中——我们的作者对“暴民”行动、反应、谋划与动态提供了扣人心弦的叙述。同样构成叙述基础的是公众舆论的角色：大多数皇帝与现代政客无异，极热衷于监测舆论并在可能时将其塑造得对自己有利。我们将看到他们并非总是成功；当“不配！”的吼声透过皇宫窗户传入皇帝耳中时，他们的日子通常屈指可数。在这一政体中，皇帝对人民负责——必要时以直接诉诸人身的方式。而这里是我们必须注意的关键点：人民似乎是在充分意识到自己有权推翻不配之统治者的情况下行动的。我们的作者身处社会上层，却也不质疑这一权利。迪米特里斯·克拉利斯（Dimitris Krallis）已结合阿塔莱亚特斯的叙述证明这一点，该叙述依托一种“共和”背景。
不存在
行动非法、或逾越其本分、或对抗上帝所设权威的任何观念。相反，普塞洛斯与阿塔莱亚特斯说人民行动仿佛受上帝驱动
（尽管他们劫掠修道院与教堂——两位史家都认为这些机构本就过于富有）。这实际上是另一种说法：他们的行动是正当的。
显然没有人（至少事后回顾时）认为人民违反对该皇帝所立的誓言，或无视皇帝受上帝任命的说法，同评判他们的行动有什么关系。
en: Our sources agree that this was a genuinely popular revolt in which all classes of the City participated, including even women. It was not orchestrated by anyone in particular—the sisters were only caught up in it—and our authors provide gripping narratives of “mob” action, reactions, planning, and dynamics. Also fundamental to the narrative is the role of public opinion: most emperors, no less than modern politicians, were extremely keen to monitor it and shape it, if possible, in their favor. We will see that they were not always successful, and when a roar of “Unworthy!” reached the emperors’ ears through the palace windows, their days were usually numbered. In this polity, emperors were answerable to the people, in a directly physical way if it came to it. And here is the key point that we must observe: the people seem to have acted in full cognizance of their right to take down an unworthy ruler. Nor do our authors, who belonged to the upper levels of society, question that right. Dimitris Krallis has demonstrated this in connection with Atteleiates’s narrative, which draws on a “republican” background.
There was no notion that the
was acting illegally, or above its station, or against an authority constituted by God. To the contrary, Psellos and Attaleiates state that the people acted as if impelled by God

(despite the fact that they plundered monasteries and churches, which, both historians believed, were too wealthy to begin with). This was effectively another way of saying that their actions were legitimate.

Apparently no one, at least in retrospect, thought it relevant that the people were violating the loyalty oaths they had sworn to that emperor or disregarding the idea that the emperor was appointed to rule by God.

zh: “全体人民”一旦达成反对某皇帝的共识，他就不再正当。毕竟最初正是他们通过即位时的欢呼使他正当。普塞洛斯以提及
的
来表达这种对称（与悖论）：米海尔五世在统治之初被引入其中，而后又提及把他推倒的“盛大而极为公开的
（秘仪）”，即
的行动（该词为 δημοσιώτατον）。
当史料提到群众对皇帝的“非难”（δυσφημία）时，他们指的是最初对他“欢呼”（εὐφημία）的在政治仪式中正相反的举动。正如贝克（Beck）所证明，这正是他们表明他在自己眼中不再配皇位的方式。
第5章将看到许多此类例子。
en: The moment the “entire people” reached a point of consensus against an emperor, he was legitimate no longer. It was they, after all, who had made him legitimate in the first place, by acclamations at his accession. Psellos expressed this symmetry (and paradox) by referring to the
of the
into which Michael V was inducted at the start of his reign and then later again to “the great and most public
” that brought him down, that is, the action by the
(the word is δημοσιώτατον).

When the sources refer to the crowd’s “disapprobation” of an emperor (δυσφημία), they mean the technical opposite of their original “acclamation” (εὐφημία) of him. As Beck demonstrated, this was how they indicated that he was no longer worthy of the throne in their eyes.
We will see many examples of this in Chapter 5.

zh: 在拜占庭，反抗正当即位的皇帝，被称为“僭逆”（tyranny）——前提是说话者站在现统治者一边。这完全取决于视角：叛乱期间双方都自认合法、视对方为暴君。哪个标签最终胜出由成败决定。本例中人民是被视为以“僭逆”的身份行事，但由于
也是皇帝选举的最终仲裁者与正当性之源，其共识立即使
成为“暴君”。普塞洛斯以一个悖论妙述此点：“平民群众是对已成为暴君者的反暴君（τὸ δ᾽ ἀγοραῖον γένος... ἀντιτυραννῆσον τῷ τυραννεύσαντι）。”
当然米海尔五世的情况更复杂，因为他对付的是比他更正当的佐伊。那已使他在人民眼中成为暴君。这位原本正当即位的皇帝违反誓言、以“例外状态”之权对付佐伊。人民随后干预以（重）建他们想要的秩序时，做了完全相同的事。他们也违反（对米海尔的）誓言并设立自己的例外状态。但他们并非简单恢复米海尔五世之前的王朝现状。塞奥多拉被从修道院拖到圣索菲亚大教堂，在那里“她被欢呼为女皇……不仅由全体
，也由所有显贵”。
她此前已享有皇帝尊荣，但如今人民行使权利授予她完整的皇帝位阶。佐伊现在必须应对这一她不乐见的局面，因为她与妹妹关系不睦。斯基利齐斯说她想排挤塞奥多拉，“但被群众阻止，群众要求她与妹妹共同统治”。
因此正是人民定义了
在近期如何重建，违背其被保护者佐伊的意愿，而无人质疑他们如此做的权利。
en: Rebellion against a lawfully constituted emperor was called a “tyranny” in Byzantium, assuming the person speaking sided with the existing ruler. This was exclusively a function of perspective: during rebellions, both sides considered themselves to be lawful and the opposing side to consist of tyrants. Which label would finally prevail was determined by success or failure. In this case, the people were acting in a “tyrannical” capacity, but because the
was also the ultimate arbiter of imperial elections and the source of legitimacy, its consensus instantly made
into the “tyrant.” Psellos expressed this nicely in a paradox: “the common crowd was a counter-tyrant to him who had already become tyrant (τὸ δ᾽ ἀγοραῖον γένος... ἀντιτυραννῆσον τῷ τυραννεύσαντι).”

The case of Michael V is more complicated, of course, because he had moved against Zoe, who was more legitimate than him. That already made him a tyrant in the eyes of the people. A duly constituted emperor had violated his oaths and acted in a “state of exception” against Zoe. The people then did exactly the same when they intervened to (re-)create the order that they wanted. They too violated their oaths (to Michael) and instituted their own state of exception. But they did not simply restore the dynastic status quo before Michael V. Theodora was dragged from her convent to Hagia Sophia, where “she was acclaimed empress... not only by the entire
but by all the notables as well.”

She had enjoyed imperial honors before, but now the people exercised their right to endow her with full imperial rank. Zoe now had to cope with this situation, which was not to her liking, for she and her sister had not been on good terms. Skylitzes says that she wanted to push Theodora out “but was prevented by the crowd, which demanded that she rule in conjunction with her.”
It was the people, then, who defined how the
would be reconstituted for the near future, against the wishes of their protégé Zoe, and no one challenged their right to do so.

zh: 当人民“一致”行动时，他们处于一个超越服从或遵从合法权威的领域，恰恰因为他们
政体，能在危机时刻直接决定自己想要什么。毕竟这正是他们欢呼新皇帝的前提。他们的共识压倒法律与先前承诺：誓言被无视、先前拥立皇帝的欢呼随之失效。换言之，当人民以单一政治行动者身份行动时，拜占庭就进入其“例外状态”的第二种类型。我们可以犬儒地怀疑民众行动背后有特殊利益，有时确实如此。但这对一切时代的政治行动者都成立。重要的是界定此类行动的意识形态框架，即在共和国眼中创造正当性的东西。
en: When the people acted “unanimously” they were set in a realm beyond obedience or deference to lawful authority precisely because they

the polity and could, in a moment of crisis, directly decide what they wanted. This was the premise behind their acclamation of new emperors, after all. Their consensus overrode law and prior commitments: oaths were ignored and past acclamations canceled. Put differently, when the people acted as a single agent in a political capacity, Byzantium would enter the second type of its “states of exception.” We can be cynical and suspect that special interests lay behind popular actions, and sometimes they did. But this is true of political agents at all times. What matters is the ideological framework that defined such actions, what created legitimacy in the eyes of the republic.

zh: 一个主权模型
en: A Model of Sovereignty

zh: 正如我们将看到的，上述事件就民众干预拜占庭政治而言只是冰山一角。但它们初步支持这一结论：人民立废皇帝的权利不受质疑，皇帝若轻视这项权利，后果须自行承担。现在我们必须把这与我们已得出的其他结论结合：皇帝为其统治与具体政策给出的主要正当化理由是它们造福罗马人民（从而取悦上帝）；皇帝不被视为权力的所有者，而被理解为从罗马人民那里受托持有它；国家机构的职能由“公共利益”决定、为促进公共善而存在。下一节将看到：皇帝只有经人民欢呼才正当，即其“选举”经民众集会的一致共识批准。所有这一切使拜占庭成为共和国的极佳候选。一个更明确的主权理论或有助于澄清根本问题。
en: As we will see, the events recounted above were only the tip of the iceberg when it came to popular interventions in Byzantine politics. Still, they give preliminary support to the conclusion that the people’s right to make and unmake emperors was not questioned, and was slighted at the emperors’ peril. This we must now combine with the other conclusions that we have drawn, namely, that the main justification that emperors gave for their rule and specific policies was that they benefited the Roman people (and thereby pleased God); that the emperors were not seen as the proprietors of power but were understood to hold it in trust from the Roman people; and that the state apparatus was a function of the “public interest” and existed to promote the common good. In the following section, we will see that emperors were legitimate only when they had been acclaimed by the people, that is, when their “election” had been ratified by universal consensus in a popular assembly. All this, then, makes Byzantium an excellent candidate for being a republic. A more explicit theory of sovereignty may help to clarify the fundamental issues.

zh: “主权”一词被学者用于许多语境与含义。开头须作初步区分。我在这里不关心作为国际关系因素的主权，即一国是否尊重（或不尊重）另一国的“自主”、或承认其在世界舞台上的权利，

而关心一个政治统一的社会——本例中即拜占庭——如何在国内政治舞台上为其政治制度的正当性奠基。在此意义上，该词常被现代史家使用但含义松散。就拜占庭而言，主权通常被归于皇帝，理由是他掌握一切合法权力——至少当政体稳定、史料给出他普遍“主事”的印象时。这是主权的松散含义，部分因为它忽视政体不稳定、被推翻、受挑战或处于过渡时发生的事——那时更根本的因素浮现；总之因为它不看政体正当性的根据、只看权力的行使者。
我只知道一次更精确判定拜占庭谁拥有主权的尝试，即贝克（Beck），他结论是人民拥有主权。贝克是一位考察拜占庭政体各要素之间正当性关系的历史学家，而非寻找最显眼的权力持有者。
en: The term “sovereignty” is used by scholars in many contexts and senses. We must make a preliminary distinction at the start. I am not interested here in sovereignty as a factor in international relations, that is, in whether one state respects (or not) the “autonomy” of another or recognizes its rights on the world stage,

but in how a politically unified society, in our case Byzantium, grounded the legitimacy of its political institutions on the domestic political stage. In this sense, the term is used often by modern historians but in a loose sense. In the Byzantine case, sovereignty is typically ascribed to the emperor on the grounds that he wielded all lawful power, at least when the regime was stable and our sources give the impression that he was generally “in charge.” This is a loose meaning of sovereignty in part because it overlooks what happened when the regime was not stable, was being toppled, challenged, or in transition, at which point more fundamental factors came to the fore; in sum, because it does not look at the grounds of the regime’s legitimacy but only at the wielders of power.

I know of only one attempt, by Beck, to ascertain more precisely who was sovereign in Byzantium, and he concluded that the people were sovereign. Beck was a historian looking at the relations of legitimacy between the elements of the Byzantine polity, not for the most visible power-holder.

zh: 诚然，拜占庭人从未发展出明确处理这一问题的宪制理论。若被问政体中谁有最终决定权，他们大多可能想到皇帝或上帝，但那不是框定问题的精确方式。我们面前的问题不是政体在和平时期如何治理。当然人民被期望服务皇帝，这一关系由话语、法律与政治实践强化；但同时皇帝也被期望反过来服务人民，这一关系由另一套话语和实践表达，并形成了相应的规范。这些关系互补却不对称，故不能同构比较。双方在一个基本意义上也不平等：在
意识形态内，正当性从人民流向权力持有者，绝不反向；事实上我们无法想象反向在罗马语境中会是什么样子。而且在理想形式中它们只在政治稳定期如此运作，即并非拜占庭的所有时间。该问的正确问题是：皇帝有权不经人民同意而统治吗？他们有权违背臣民利益行动吗？若人民判定某皇帝不再为其利益行动，他们有权废黜他吗？这些问题把我们引向正确方向。
en: To be sure, the Byzantines never developed a constitutional theory that explicitly addressed this question. If asked who had the final say in the polity, most of them would probably think of the emperor or God, but that would not be a precise way to frame the question. The question before us is not how the polity was governed in times of peace. Certainly the people were expected to serve the emperor, and this relationship was reinforced by discursive, legal, and political practices; but at the same time the emperor was also supposed, in turn, to serve the people, a relationship that was expressed and codified in different discourses and practices. These relationships were complementary and yet also asymmetrical, so they cannot be homologically compared. The two parties were also unequal in a basic sense, which is that within the ideology of the

legitimacy flowed from the people to the holders of power and never the reverse; indeed, we cannot imagine what the reverse might look like in a Roman context. Moreover, in their ideal form they operated like this only in periods of political stability, which is to say not all the time in Byzantium. The right questions to ask would be: Did emperors have the right to rule without popular consent? Did they have the right to act against the interests of their subjects? And, if the people decided that an emperor was no longer acting in their interests, did they have the right to depose him? These questions point us in the right direction.

zh: 卡尔·施米特（Carl Schmitt）提供了类似的框定方式。依施米特，主权者是决定何时进入紧急状态者——阿甘本（Agamben）称之为“例外状态”。谁能援引非常情势以实施紧急措施、超越法律所定义的常态框架，谁就是政治领域的真正主人。
我们已看到皇帝能在该框架之外运作，但人们理解他只能为促进臣民之善而如此。另一方面，人民能够且确实暂停法治以摆脱他们不喜欢的皇帝，并在该例外状态内任命任何他们想要的人接替。那些时刻的法律暂停超越了对现任皇帝的否定、因而也超越了对他一切效忠誓言的撕毁。它还常常伴随劫掠宅邸、教堂与修道院，焚毁政府建筑，释放
中的囚犯，私刑处死不受欢迎的高官。所有这一切不受惩罚，部分因为下一任皇帝不能事后把拥他上台的事件定为非法，部分也因为它们恰恰发生在法律秩序被暂停之时——即不存在正当的“法律秩序”。我们已看到足够多此类实例，为总论题提供初步支持；第5章将进一步充实其历史。
en: Carl Schmitt provides a similar way to frame the issue. According to Schmitt, the sovereign is the one who decides when there is a state of emergency, which Agamben called a “state of exception.” He who can invoke extraordinary circumstances in order to implement emergency measures, above and beyond the framework of normality defined by the laws, is the true master of the political sphere.

We have seen that the emperor could operate outside that framework but it was understood that he could do so only in order to promote the good of his subjects. The people, on the other hand, could and did suspend the rule of law in order to rid themselves of an emperor whom they did not like and, within that state of exception, appoint whomever they wanted as his replacement. The suspension of law at those moments went beyond the repudiation of the current emperor and, therefore, the breaking of all oaths of loyalty to him. It also often entailed the looting of mansions, churches, and monasteries, the burning down of government buildings, freeing the prisoners in the

and lynching unpopular high officials. All this was done with impunity in part because the next emperor could not retroactively treat the events that brought him to the throne as illegal, but in part also because they occurred precisely when the order of law was suspended; that is, there was no legitimate “lawful order.” We have seen enough instances of that already to provide prima facie support for the general thesis, and Chapter 5 will further flesh out its history.

zh: 简言之，就当前目的而言，我们不可把主权与政府混淆——政府即人民委托给皇帝行使的官方权力。这一区分由现代共和主义理论家阐明，而其理论最契合拜占庭者，讽刺而妙趣横生地，是卢梭（Rousseau）。鉴于他对拜占庭的看法，他听到这话会惊骇，
但他及其时代对它其实知之甚少。启蒙思想家倾向把它当作一面镜子，映照并弃绝他们自己社会中想要废除的那些方面。他们的“拜占庭”观念是有用的论战工具，而非学术建构。使卢梭有用的是他对罗马共和传统的理论化。碰巧——尽管他不知道——拜占庭正是该传统的后期阶段。
en: In short, for our present purposes, we must not confuse sovereignty with the government, that is, the wielding of official power that is delegated to the emperors by the people. The distinction was made clear by modern theorists of republicanism, and the one whose theory fits Byzantium best is, ironically and deliciously, Rousseau. He would be horrified to hear that, given what he believed about Byzantium,

but he and his age really knew little about it. The thinkers of the Enlightenment tended to treat it as a mirror in which to reflect and abjure those aspects of their own societies that they wanted to abolish. Their idea of “Byzantium” was a useful polemical tool, not a scholarly construct. What makes Rousseau useful is that he theorized the Roman republican tradition. It just so happens, though he did not know it, that Byzantium was a later phase of that tradition.

zh: 在其《社会契约论》（
）开头，卢梭呼应西塞罗对
的定义，声称：
en: At the beginning of his
Rousseau echoes Cicero’s definition of the
when he claims that:

zh: 制服一群人与治理一个社会之间永远存在巨大差别。“当分散的人无论数目多少被相继奴役于单一个人时，我在此只看到主人与奴隶，看不到人民及其首领；如果你愿意，这是一种聚合，而非结合；这里既无公共善，也无政治体……人民在把自己交托给国王之前就已经是人民。”
en: there will always be a great difference between subjugating a multitude and ruling a society. When scattered men, regardless of their number, are successively enslaved to a single man, I see in this nothing but a master and slaves, I do not see in it a people and its chief; it is, if you will, an aggregation, but not an association; there is here neither public good, nor body politic... A people is a people before giving itself to a king.

zh: 那种“聚合”正是普里斯科斯（Priskos）等罗马作家就认为，阿提拉的帝国不过是这样一种聚合；它不是一个真正的
。相比之下，罗曼尼亚（Romanía）由广泛共识统一，宗教只是其中一个方面。卢梭说此类政体中最重要的法律不是写下来的、而是“在公民心中；这才是国家真正的宪法……我指的是道德、习俗，尤其是舆论”，由此表明自己是古典而非现代思想家。
罗曼尼亚的道德共识正是这样一部宪法；它不是成文之物。它的模式与秩序对研究行动中社会的历史学家更可见，对法学者较不可见——至少就后者主要处理法律文本而言。对局限于宫廷宣传的学者更不可见。下文还将考虑“舆论”在塑造拜占庭权力行使中的至高角色，尽管上述插曲已多次触及。
en: That “aggregation” is what Roman writers like Priskos believed, say, the empire of Attila was; it was not a proper

By contrast, Romanía was unified by a broad consensus of which religion was only one aspect. Rousseau reveals himself a classical rather than a modern thinker when he says that the most important laws in such a polity are not those that are written down but are “in the hearts of the citizens; which is the State’s genuine constitution... I speak of morals, customs, and above all of opinion.”

The moral consensus of Romanía was such a constitution; it was not something set down in writing. Its modes and orders are more visible to the historian, who studies the society in action, and less so to the legal scholar, at least insofar as the latter deals primarily with legal texts. It is even less visible to scholars who limit themselves to court propaganda. Below we will also consider the supreme role of “opinion” in shaping the exercise of power in Byzantium, though the episodes presented above have often touched on it.

zh: 卢梭解释说共和国不由特定政府类型定义。“我称任何由法律统治的国家为共和国，不论治理形式如何，因为那时唯有公共利益能左右统治，
才有意义。一切正当政府都是共和的。”他在关于最后一词的关键注释中补充：“此词我不仅理解为贵族制或民主制，而泛指任何由公意——即法律——引导的政府。要正当，政府不可与主权者混淆，而须是其臣仆：那时君主制本身也是共和国。”
如我们已指出，君主制的事实不应妨碍我们把拜占庭视为共和国。这对统治者地位有关键意涵：“那些主张人民把自己服从于首领的行为不是契约的人完全正确。它绝对只是一种委托、一种职分：他们作为主权者的单纯官员，以其名义行使它授予他们的权力。”

主权者与其政府不是可彼此订约的同构实体。权力被委托，但非无条件；上一节我们见证了主权者从其政府收回权力的时刻——卢梭以形式术语理论化了这种可能：“人民一旦合法地作为主权体集会，政府的一切管辖权即告终止。”除批准皇帝选举的集会外，拜占庭缺乏“合法”民众集会——若该词指卢梭所设想的瑞士模式正式召集机构。民众行动通常“法外”，但那不使其“不正当”；恰恰相反。它是一种法律事实暂停的状态，其间真正的主权者——人民——行使原始政治权威。回到卢梭：“这些［政府权力］暂停的间隔，当君主［国王］承认或不得不承认一个实际上级时，总是对它构成威胁；而这些作为政治体之盾与政府之缰的人民集会，历来是令执政者心生恐惧。”
让我们在此想象一位拜占庭皇帝听见二三十万张嘴在皇宫窗外高呼“不配！”。
en: Rousseau explains that republics are not defined by a particular type of government. “I call republic any state ruled by laws, whatever may be the form of administration: for then the public interest alone governs and the

counts for something. Every legitimate government is republican.” He adds in a crucial note on the last word: “By this word I understand not only aristocracy or a democracy, but in general any government guided by the general will, which is the law. To be legitimate, the government must not be confused with the sovereign, but be its minister: then monarchy itself is a republic.”

As we have noted, the fact of monarchy should not hinder us from viewing Byzantium as a republic. This has crucial implications for the position of the ruler: “Those who contend that the act by which a people subjects itself to chiefs is not a contract are perfectly right. It is absolutely nothing but a commission, an office in which they, as mere officers of the sovereign, exercise in its name the power it has vested in them.”

The sovereign and his government were not homologous entities, such as could enter into a contract with each other. Powers were delegated, but not unconditionally, and in the previous section we witnessed a moment when the sovereign took power back from his government, an eventuality that Rousseau theorized in formal terms: “The instant the people is legitimately assembled as a sovereign body, all jurisdiction of the government ceases.” With the exception of assemblies to ratify imperial elections, Byzantium lacked “legitimate” popular assemblies, if that refers to formally convoked institutions on the Swiss model that Rousseau envisaged. Popular action was usually “extralegal,” but that did not make it “illegitimate”; quite the contrary. It was a state of de facto suspension of the laws during which the true sovereign, the people, exercised raw political authority. To return to Rousseau, “these intervals of suspension [of the powers of the government], when the prince [king] recognizes or has to recognize an actual superior have always been threatening to it, and these assemblies of the people which are the shield of the body politic and the curb of the government have at all times been the dread of chiefs.”
Let us here imagine a Byzantine emperor hearing two or three hundred thousand mouths chant “Unworthy!” outside his palace windows.

zh: 卢梭对政府与主权者的区分、他对罗马
道德或习俗基础的阐明、以及他关于政府为君主制时主权仍可在民的模型，使他的思想足以纠正许多历史学家习惯使用的“国家”概念中所含的霍布斯（Hobbes）式前提。上文我们已见霍布斯把国家视为在概念上可与它所统治的人民分离。
霍布斯不允许主权者与政府分离。在《利维坦》（
）中，人民自身没有主权权威；他们彼此同意把它托付给君主，基本上由此把它创造出来，却从不拥有它。因此他们无权收回或转移它：“臣属于君主者，未经其许可不能抛弃君主制、回到一盘散沙的混乱状态，也不能把原由此人代表的共同人格改托给另一人或另一个团体。”
显然拜占庭人不是霍布斯主义者。他们的
不因皇帝被推翻、皇冠转移而解散，人民也不变成“分散的群众”。他们是主权性的
。但霍布斯不同于卢梭，没有设想过可以不依靠君主、凭共同的风俗（
）形成一个人民：他以抽象的、法律定义的权力关系思考。他说君主“无论做什么都不能伤害任何臣民；也不应被任何臣民指控不义”，这也远离罗马思维方式。
霍布斯基本上把这一点
为如此。在他看来臣民不允许质疑或辱骂君主。
相比之下，在拜占庭传统中几乎没有一个皇帝不被指控不义；第5章将考察民众辱骂皇帝的诸多方式。霍布斯提及罗马对其理论的替代方案时说：选举产生的国王与权力受限的国王“不是主权者，而是主权者的臣仆”，因为“若知道谁有权在他死后授予主权，也就知道主权此前就在他们之中……因此主权始终在那个有权限制他的集会之中”。
换言之，霍布斯承认罗马传统中主权权力居于人民，尽管他没有展开这对罗马
史——即拜占庭——可能意味着什么。
在他看来，“放肆地控制主权者行动”的努力按定义不正当，且源于读太多希腊罗马文学。
en: Rousseau’s distinction between government and sovereign, his explication of the moral or customary grounds of a Roman

and his model for how the sovereignty may still be popular when the government is monarchical make his thought an antidote to the Hobbesian notions that permeate the concept of “the state” that many historians intuitively use. We saw above Hobbes’s view of the state as conceptually separable from the people over which it ruled.
Hobbes did not allow for a separation between the sovereign and the government. In the

the people by themselves have no sovereign authority; in agreeing among themselves to entrust it to the monarch they basically bring it into being, but never own it. They therefore have no right to take it back or transfer it: “they that are subjects to a monarch, cannot without his leave cast off monarchy, and return to the confusion of a disunited multitude; nor transfer their person from him that beareth it, to another man, or other assembly of men.”
Clearly, the Byzantines were not Hobbesians. Their
was not dissolved when an emperor was taken down and the crown transferred, nor did the people become a “disunited multitude.” They were the sovereign
But Hobbes, unlike Rousseau, had no conception of the

that can create a people apart from their monarch: he thought in terms of abstract relations of power, legally defined. He was also far from the Roman way of thinking when he said this about the monarch: “whatever he do, it can be no injury to any of his subjects; nor ought he to be by any of them accused of injustice.”
Hobbes basically
this to be the case. In his view, subjects are not allowed to question or abuse the monarch.

In the Byzantine tradition, by contrast, there was hardly a single emperor not accused of injustice, and we will consider in Chapter 5 the many ways in which the populace abused emperors. Hobbes alludes to Roman alternatives to his theory when he says that elective kings and kings with limited power “are not sovereigns, but ministers of the sovereign,” because “if it be known who have the power to give the sovereignty after his death, it is known also that the sovereignty was in them before... The sovereignty therefore was always in that assembly which had the right to limit him.”
In other words, Hobbes recognized that in Roman tradition the sovereign power resided in the people, though he did not elaborate on what this might have meant for Roman
history, that is, Byzantium.
In his view, efforts to “licentiously control the action of sovereigns” were illegitimate by definition and stemmed from reading too much Greek and Roman literature.

zh: 也许不如应有的那样广为人知的是：早期帝国中，权力在每位皇帝即位时正式从元老院与人民转移给他。皇帝权威奠基于一部特定立法（或一组立法），称
，它依共和国的职官与惯例规定皇帝的确切权力。如今仅存韦斯巴芗（Vespasian）的那部，但每位皇帝即位时都会获颁一部新的授权法，其措辞重复前任，至少到3世纪早期。似乎公民大会——如今是“无害的仪式”——批准这些
我们或许想把它当作法律虚构而不予理会，但首先须弄清虚构究竟何在。当然到此人民与元老院在此事上选择余地很小，故这些不是任何现代意义上的自由集会（然而我们自己的选举很可能在那意义上也是虚构）。
但君主制自创立伊始，就有深厚的民众基础，也由此取得了正当性。正如怀斯曼（T. P. Wiseman）所写，恺撒的权力：
en: It is perhaps not as well known as it should be that in the early empire power was formally transferred from the senate and people to each emperor upon his accession. Imperial authority was grounded in a specific enactment (or a set of them) called a

that stipulated an emperor’s exact powers in terms of the offices and conventions of the Republic. Only that of Vespasian now survives, but a new one was passed for each emperor, its wording repeating that of his predecessors, until at least the early third century. It seems that comitial assemblies—now “harmless ceremonies”—ratified these

We might be tempted to dismiss this as a legal fiction, but we first have to be clear where the fiction resides. Certainly, by this point the people and senate had little choice in the matter, so these were not free assemblies in any modern sense (however, it is likely that our own elections are also fictions in that sense).
But the origin of the monarchy had a strong populist rationale, and legitimacy. As T. P. Wiseman has written, Caesar’s powers:

zh: 全部由罗马人民投票授予，没有理由想象人民被贿赂或胁迫。恺撒的权力不是篡夺，而是由唯一有资格者依宪授予。当然资深
认为共和国已死，因为他们自己的行动自由被削减。而削减他们的行动自由正是罗马人民想要的。

thought the republic was dead, because their own freedom of action was curtailed. Curtailing their freedom of action was what the Roman People wanted.

zh: 而且早期帝国中这些民众集会被认为必要、以授予帝国政体正当性，这一事实本身表明正当性确实奠基在人民同意之上：至少这一点不是虚构。正如布伦特（Brunt）在其
研究中指出，“任何独裁者都必须记住臣民会容忍什么”，
而是共和意识形态先于政治事实规定了什么可容忍、什么不可。拜占庭历史上皇位继承的实际展开方式——无论稳定还是动荡实例——表明我们或许想当作虚构而不予理会的东西实际上是政体意识形态的根深蒂固方面。
en: Moreover, the very fact that these popular assemblies were deemed necessary in the first place during the early empire to grant legitimacy to the imperial regime indicates that legitimacy was indeed grounded in popular consent: this, at least, was no fiction. As Brunt noted in his study of the
“any autocrat had to bear in mind what his subjects would tolerate,”

and it was republican ideology, prior to political fact, which dictated what was tolerable and what not. The way in which the succession to imperial power played out historically in Byzantium, in both stable and tumultuous instances, reveals that what we might be tempted to dismiss as a fiction was actually a deep-seated aspect of the polity’s ideology.

zh: “从一开始，”坎贝尔（J. B. Campbell）写道，帝国“就是宪制形式与合法性框架内的绝对君主制”。
en: “From the start,” wrote J. B. Campbell, the empire “had been an absolute monarchy in a framework of constitutional formality and legality.”

zh: 而且由于皇权在法律与道德上都被理解为相对
及其所有者
而言，可以说“形式主权仍居于”人民：“这里的问题是
的形式结构及其组成部分的关系，而非政治权力实际位置的问题。”
保罗·韦纳（Paul Veyne）在一部近期权威性的罗马帝国综述开头指出，“恺撒们的政体与我们最熟悉的君主制非常不同”。具体而言，皇帝“不是作为所有者占据皇位，而是受共同体委托来领导共和国”。韦纳反复称此为虚构，但也承认它的存在防止了职位的权威被个人篡夺：它只能由人民委托。皇帝理论上作为共和国的公仆统治，“不是为他自己的荣耀、如国王那样，而是为罗马人的荣耀”。
这当然解释了我们已在拜占庭案例中看到的皇帝与政体关系的许多方面；韦纳补充说人民主权学说持续到拜占庭终结。然而奇怪的是，愿意承认这一点的史家如此之少，更不用说把它作为拜占庭史研究的基础了。
en: Moreover, as imperial power was understood legally as well as morally in relation to the
and its owner, the
it can be said that “formal sovereignty still resided” with the people: “What is at issue here is the formal structure of the
and the relations of its component parts, not the question of the real location of political power.”

Paul Veyne begins a recent magisterial survey of the Roman empire by noting that “the regime of the Caesars was very different from the monarchies with which we are most familiar.” Specifically, the emperor “did not occupy the throne as a proprietor, but as someone mandated by the collectivity, charged by it to direct the republic.” Veyne repeatedly calls this a fiction but also concedes that its existence prevented the authority of the position from being usurped by the person: it could only be delegated by the people. The emperor ruled in theory as the servant of the republic, “not for his own glory, in the fashion of a king, but for the glory of the Romans.”

This, of course, explains much about the relationship between the emperor and the polity that we have already seen in the Byzantine case, and Veyne adds that the doctrine of popular sovereignty lasted to the end of Byzantium. Still, it is strange how few historians have been willing to admit this, to say nothing of making it the basis for their research into Byzantine history.

当然查士丁尼也声称依上帝权威统治；第6章将考察这两种沿不同轨道运行的皇权观念的不安融合。从《民法大全》（

zh: 依其

这一根本逻辑在拜占庭被充分理解。12世纪诗体编年史家君士坦丁·马纳塞斯（Konstantinos Manasses）让全体罗马人集会投票废除君主制、在共和国创立时设立执政官。
这是
的反面却与之完美互补。在科穆宁（Komnenoi）朝下，人们可能相信罗马
拥有如此主权权力。但除此类具体实例外，君主之镜中一个老生常谈是：皇帝统治的基础在于人民同意。1080年代，塞奥菲拉克托斯（Theophylaktos）——已任或即将任保加利亚大主教——在一部著作中向潜在皇位继承人解释：
一词来自 βάσις οὖσα λαοῦ，“以人民为根基”，字面作“人民的基础”（相比之下
是“当全体人民对

暴君与合法
的关键区别在于：暴君不从人民接受权力之缰，而是凭武力自夺。
相反
